How fit() compares the simulation with the observations: the loss

Source: R/finn-loss-doc.R
finn_loss.Rd

fit() estimates the parameters by making the simulation match the observations. "Match" is measured by the loss: for each of the six responses – dbh, ba, trees, growth, mortality, regeneration – the simulated value of every site, census year and species is compared with the observed one through a likelihood, the six comparisons are added up, and fit() lowers that sum. This page explains the arguments of fit() that set the comparison: loss_family, loss_aggregation, loss_resolution, loss_weights and weight_scale, loss_recruit, and tree_data. Their defaults are robust in most cases: a first fit needs none of them.

The six responses and their likelihoods (loss_family)

Each response has its own likelihood, chosen for the kind of number it is. The defaults, following Pichler & Käber (2026):

responsewhat is compareddefaultalternatives
dbhmean diameter, cm"mse" (squared error)"gaussian", "none"
babasal area per patch"mse""gaussian", "none"
treesnumber of trees per patch"poisson" (a count)"nbinom", "mse", "none"
growthmean annual relative growth rate"mse""gaussian", "none"
mortalityshare of the trees that died, 0 to 1"binomial""mse", "gaussian", "poisson", "none"
regenerationrecruits per hectare over the interval"nbinom" (an overdispersed count)"poisson", "mse", "gaussian", "none"

loss_family is a named character vector; name only what departs from the defaults, e.g. loss_family = c(trees = "nbinom"). "mse" is the squared error, equivalent to a Gaussian likelihood with a fixed variance; "gaussian" additionally estimates the variance. "binomial" is the Bernoulli/binomial likelihood for a proportion in [0, 1] (the model predicts the probability of dying through a sigmoid), weighted by the number of trees at risk when data carries n_at_risk; it respects the bounds and the mean-variance link of a proportion, which "mse" ignores. "nbinom" is implemented for trees and regeneration only. "none" switches a response off: it contributes nothing and needs no column in data – use it when a response was not observed, or when its information enters through another term (e.g. dbh = "none" and ba = "none" once the size distribution is scored through size classes, below).

The rates are compared over the observation interval: with period_length in data, the simulated yearly growth and mortality are compounded into one rate per year (the geometric mean of 1 + g, one minus the geometric mean survival – as makeObsData() derives the observed rates) and simulated recruitment is summed, before they meet the observation (see finn_data and fit()). Growth is compared as a relative rate (dbh / dbh_before - 1), the model's own quantity; training against the absolute increment was tested and was worse and more seed-variable, because it couples the growth parameters to whichever trees happen to be present. finn(growth_rate = ) says whether the observed growth is a rate per time step or the increment over the whole interval.

For regeneration, "nbinom" (the default) uses the recruit dispersion theta of the regeneration process and applies finn(recruit_obs_weight = ); "poisson" has no dispersion parameter, so it cannot collapse, but in 0.2.0 it ignores recruit_obs_weight and scores per-hectare values, with trees_offset added to the prediction. See recruitment.

A missing observation (NA) is left out of its term; the other responses of that cell are still scored. A term that is not finite at a step (an overflowing likelihood) is dropped from that step with the default fit(nonfinite = "drop_term") and counted in model$nonfinite_counts.

Balancing the six terms (loss_weights, weight_scale)

The six terms are summed, and their raw sizes differ by orders of magnitude: on the bundled FIA data dbh is a squared error in cm2 (about 430 at the start) while growth is a squared error on a ratio (about 0.03). Summed as they are, dbh would take 87 % of the objective and growth 1 %, and growth would never improve.

loss_weights = "auto" (the default) fixes this without knowing the units. Each term is divided by its intercept-only baseline: the loss that predicting the single best constant (the mean of the observations) would get. Every term then measures the same thing on the same scale, the fraction of its own null deviance. For a squared error the baseline is the variance of the observations, so this is scaling by 1 / var(y); for the Poisson, negative-binomial and binomial terms it is the corresponding null deviance, where a standard deviation would be the wrong scale. The baselines are stored in model$loss_baseline, the resulting weights in model$loss_weights, and every fit reports each response's share of the objective at the baseline. It is a weighting for a balanced objective, not the joint likelihood of the six responses.

A useful side effect: the per-response values in model$history read directly as "how much better than the mean" – 1 is no better than the intercept, below 1 is better, above 1 is worse.

A numeric loss_weights vector (six numbers, in the order dbh, ba, trees, growth, mortality, regeneration) multiplies the balanced terms, so each number reads as that response's relative share: c(1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1) gives growth twice the weight of every other response. On the FIA example, balancing the objective is worth about +0.24 Spearman correlation on held-out growth, more than tuning lr or epochs (vignette Fitting FINN to FIA data). weight_scale = FALSE (or "raw") applies the vector to the raw, unbalanced terms instead – the meaning the argument weights had before 0.2.0, kept for reproducing earlier analyses; the shares are reported in both modes.

How cohorts become the compared quantity (loss_aggregation)

The simulation works on cohorts; the observation is one number per site, year and species. loss_aggregation says how the cohorts are summarised before the comparison, per response, as a named character vector or – for a type that needs settings – a named list. Anything not named keeps its default, so the argument only ever states what departs from it:

  • "mean" – the abundance-weighted mean over the cohorts of a site and species. The default for dbh, growth and mortality.

  • "sum" – the sum over cohorts. The default for ba, trees and regeneration.

  • "size_classes" – stem counts per diameter class, for trees only. Needs breaks (the class boundaries in cm) and optionally tau (the softness of the class edges in cm, default 1). K breaks give K + 1 classes, read from the columns n_class_1, ..., n_class_K+1 of data. With a Poisson family this scores total abundance and size composition at once (independent Poisson class counts factorise into a Poisson total times a multinomial composition). Class membership is a difference of sigmoids rather than a hard cut, so the term stays differentiable in the diameter; small tau approaches hard binning.

  • "quantiles" – the abundance-weighted diameter quantiles instead of the mean, for dbh only. Needs probs (e.g. c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)) and optionally tau (the softness on the cumulative-abundance scale, default 0.05). The observation is read from the columns dbh_q10, dbh_q50, dbh_q90 of data (dbh_q<100*p>). Where size classes ask how many stems fall in an interval, this asks how thick the stem at a given position of the distribution is: the upper quantile speaks about the big trees that carry the basal area, which a count likelihood weighs like saplings.

  • "tree" – no aggregation: the growth and mortality equations are evaluated on the observed trees at their observed diameters, with the light of the observed stand, and compared tree by tree. For growth and mortality only; needs tree_data. See Scoring individual trees.

Example – score the size distribution through stem counts and the two rates per tree:

fit(m, data = obs_dt, env = env, tree_data = tree_obs_dt,
    loss_family      = c(dbh = "none", ba = "none"),
    loss_aggregation = list(trees  = list(type = "size_classes",
                                          breaks = seq(20, 60, by = 10)),
                            growth = "tree", mortality = "tree"))

Scoring individual trees (tree_data, loss_resolution)

By default growth and mortality are scored per site, species and census, as means over cohorts. Two options score them per tree instead; both take the tree table in tree_data (finn_data lists its columns), but they ask different questions.

loss_aggregation = c(growth = "tree", mortality = "tree") predicts each OBSERVED tree: the equations run on its measured dbh at the start of the interval with the light of the observed stand, and only the yearly environment changes across the interval. It measures the error of the growth and mortality functions alone. loss_resolution = "tree" predicts each SIMULATED cohort that started as an observed tree, along the model's own trajectory (simulated growth, competitors, light). It measures the error of the functions plus the drift of the simulated stand.

loss_aggregation = "tree"loss_resolution = "tree"
the tree isobserved: measured dbh, observed competitors, yearly environmentsimulated: the cohort it started as, along the model's trajectory
measuresthe growth and mortality functions alonethe functions plus the drift of the simulated stand
responseschosen separately, e.g. only mortality = "tree"growth and mortality together
init_cohortany, incl. binned (makeInitCohorts(dbh_binsize = ))one cohort per tree (makeInitCohorts() without dbh_binsize)
tree_data needsdbh at the interval startcohortID of the initial cohort
combines withthe simulated dbh/ba/trees/regeneration termsreanchor and teacher_forcing
diagnosticspredictTrees()$tree_deaths, $tree_pred

Use the first to estimate the process functions from the trees as observed, the second to test whether simulated trajectories follow the real trees. The two cannot be combined in one fit.

Under loss_resolution = "tree" the two terms replace the per-cell terms rather than adding to them (scoring a response twice under two weights is a redundancy the optimiser can trade against itself); the loss vector, loss_weights and $history keep their six positions. The correspondence is carried by the cohort ids: a cohort keeps the id of the slot it was created in, so cohort j of a (site, patch) is tree j of the list that generation started from; recruits get ids above that block. A generation starts at init_cohort and restarts at every anchor under reanchor/teacher_forcing. Growth is scored over the interval as the aggregate term is, mortality as the compounded probability 1 - prod(1 - m) against the tree's 0/1 fate – never the sampled death, which at one tree is a coin flip. A cohort the simulation kills inside a window is kept with trees = 0 until its generation ends, so both terms score every tree and the scored sample does not depend on the parameters; $tree_deaths reports per census and epoch how often the simulation killed a tree the inventory found alive (frac_killed), in which year (mean_kill_year), and the share that entered the window already dead (frac_ghost). With the binned competition a killed cohort still occupies a slot of the height quantiles, so createProcess(light_mask = TRUE) (the default) or continuous = TRUE is needed for the competition process; fit() warns otherwise.

Where the recruits come from (loss_recruit)

loss_recruit = "simulated" (the default) lets the regeneration process recruit, and its parameters are estimated with the rest. An inventory samples small trees sparsely, so recruitment is the hardest process to estimate jointly: a mis-fitted regeneration process feeds a wrong stand into every later interval, and growth and mortality compensate for it. loss_recruit = "observed" therefore drives the stand with the OBSERVED recruitment: reg in data divided by period_length is the expected recruitment per hectare and year in every simulated year of that interval, drawn per patch by the recruit sampler as usual. In that call the regeneration term is weighted 0, every parameter of the regeneration process is frozen (and gets its previous state back when fit() returns), and growth, mortality and competition are estimated on a stand that recruits what was observed. The regeneration process is then fitted in a call of its own, with the other processes' optimizeSpecies and optimizeEnv off. Refused: an NA reg in an interval that needs it, a simulated year in two intervals or before a site's first interval, and reanchor/teacher_forcing. simulateForest() with recruits = "observed" simulates the same way for checking such a model; recruitment has the unit chain and the staged recipe.

Reading the fit

model$history holds the six (weighted) terms per epoch, model$loss_baseline the intercept-only baselines, model$loss_weights the weights in force, and model$param_history the parameters at every checkpoints epochs. A fit has converged when the parameters stop moving, not when the losses look flat.

References

Pichler, M., & Käber, Y. (2026). Inferring processes within dynamic forest models using hybrid modelling. Methods in Ecology and Evolution. doi:10.1111/2041-210x.70347

See also

fit(), finn_data, recruitment, predictTrees()

Examples

library(data.table)
# three sites of the bundled Oregon FIA sample and two epochs per fit, to
# show the arguments; a real calibration uses all sites and many epochs
sites <- 1:3
Nsp   <- max(fia_obs_dt$species)
obs   <- fia_obs_dt[siteID %in% sites]
env   <- fia_env_dt[siteID %in% sites]
init  <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees[siteID %in% sites], Nspecies = Nsp)
FINN.seed(1)
m <- finn(N_species = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,
          growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, growth),
          mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, mortality),
          regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, regeneration_capped))

# the defaults: six likelihoods, balanced by their intercept-only baselines
fit(m, data = obs, env = env, init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L,
    patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE)
#> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0.768)
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%
m$loss_baseline   # the loss of predicting the mean, per response
#>          dbh           ba        trees       growth    mortality regeneration 
#> 4.117755e+02 8.303134e-02 1.033310e+00 5.429424e-05 2.596614e-02 1.302194e+00 
m$loss_weights    # 1 / baseline: the weight of each response
#>          dbh           ba        trees       growth    mortality regeneration 
#> 2.428508e-03 1.204364e+01 9.677641e-01 1.841816e+04 3.851170e+01 7.679345e-01 
# the six terms per epoch (1 = no better than the mean); the seventh
# column is not used
do.call(rbind, m$history)
#>           [,1]      [,2]      [,3]     [,4]     [,5]     [,6] [,7]
#> [1,] 2.1722367 0.7110548 0.5395446 28.76573 1.319534 1.362056    0
#> [2,] 0.9194432 0.3529012 0.5377366 24.79219 1.324605 1.413360    0

# another likelihood for the stem counts, and mean dbh left out of the loss
fit(m, data = obs, env = env, init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L,
    patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE,
    loss_family = c(trees = "nbinom", dbh = "none"))
#> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=1, ba=12, trees=1.09, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0.77)
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): ba=20%, trees=20%, growth=20%, mortality=20%, regeneration=20%
do.call(rbind, m$history)
#>      [,1]      [,2]      [,3]     [,4]     [,5]     [,6] [,7]
#> [1,]    0 0.5508276 0.6653778 19.75080 1.304604 1.350756    0
#> [2,]    0 0.5163020 0.6760594 23.33407 1.291273 1.401224    0

# mortality scored on every observed tree instead of on the site's rate
fit(m, data = obs, env = env, init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L,
    patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE,
    tree_data = fia_tree_dt[siteID %in% sites],
    loss_aggregation = c(mortality = "tree"))
#> ℹ Using per-site aggregation windows (one backward per batch): loss_aggregation = "tree" needs them
#> [tree_data] 113 trees, up to 14 per patch and observation year
#> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=6.53, regeneration=0.773)
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%
